title: Match Point
logline: A close local tournament match stops dead on a decision nobody accepts, and for several long minutes nobody is playing and everybody has an opinion.
human_question: In the minutes after a ruling nobody accepts, what does a crowd actually do with its own displeasure?

situation.what_happens: A closely fought match between teams who all know each other reaches a decision that one side will not take. Play stops. The protest is public and immediate, and it involves people who have no part in the game at all, because everyone watching also has a view. Someone has to get the match moving again, which means somebody's word has to be accepted by people who do not want to accept it. Then play resumes, and the same people who were loudest a moment ago are back inside the ordinary business of the game.
situation.who_is_involved: The players on both sides; the official whose word is being refused; the organisers who have to restart the match and keep the tournament running; spectators who know every player by name and have money, pride or family in the result; and whoever steps in from outside the argument to calm it.
situation.what_is_at_stake: A result, a small trophy, and a good deal of standing in a place where everyone will meet again next week. For the official, being obeyed at all. For the film, not turning ordinary people having an ordinary sporting row into evidence of bad character.
situation.how_it_unfolds: It begins with a tight game and a decision that goes one way. The pressures are the crowd's closeness, the fact that the ruling cannot be reviewed, and the minutes passing with nothing happening. It can end with the ruling standing, with it being reversed, with the match abandoned, or with an apology nobody asked for. Reality decides, and so does whether any such moment happens at all during the days a crew is present; it cannot be arranged.

concept_merge.why_together: C007 supplies the occasion in the sources' own words: Margaya lists a request refused, one's word not accepted, and others seeming to have done wrong among the everyday causes of this state [C007-M:L17], and both hate-rooted minds always carry a painful mental feeling [C007-P:L25–L28]. C022 supplies the constant floor beneath it: restlessness is one of the four present in every unwholesome moment [C022-P:L31], which is what a stopped match looks like from the boundary. Together, an occasion and its contents, at the volume a village ground gives them.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the state is public and brief at the same time. A whole ground can hold it at once, and a few minutes later the same ground is holding something else entirely, which is precisely what the scheme claims: these are moments, not people.

concept_links.why: Margaya names 'when one's word is not accepted' and 'when others seem to do wrong, or are thought to have done wrong' among the ordinary daily occasions for this state of mind [C007-M:L17], and Pradeepika's account gives its shape: a disliked object met, and a mind that strikes against it [C007-P:L32–L34], always with a painful mental feeling [C007-P:L25–L28]. A disputed ruling is that occasion in its most public and least private form. The film may not use the sources' insistence that even laughing harm is hate-rooted [C007-M:L11] to read anyone's behaviour on a sports field, and may not narrate the traditional bodily effects [C007-P:L47] as observable fact.

Restlessness is one of the four factors both sources place in every unwholesome mind, whatever else is present [C022-P:L31; C022-M:L3]. A stoppage is that unsettledness spread across a whole ground rather than held by one arguing player. The earlier version of this link compared restlessness to wind shaking the leaves of a tree; the digest records the compendium's similes and that is not among them, so the image has been dropped rather than attributed.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: The texts name having your word refused, and thinking someone else has done wrong, among the commonest reasons this heat arrives at all; and they say it never arrives without pain. A ground full of people can hold it together and lose it together in the space of a few minutes, which is a plain way of seeing that it is a state passing through people rather than a description of them.
what_must_be_real: The match, the dispute and its resolution must be a real, unstaged local event. No decision, appeal or reaction may be prompted or restaged, and no moment may be waited for as an opportunity. Anyone shown at their angriest must consent to being shown that way, and the aftermath must be filmed with the same weight as the flare.
position_hint: middle, if it were used: it is the group's most public and least intimate version of the same state, and it works best after the state has been introduced somewhere quieter. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Editing could make ordinary players look like people with a permanent bad temper, which is exactly the reading the scheme forbids.
Consent from spectators shown reacting strongly.
Exaggerating a brief stoppage into more drama than it actually was.
The event cannot be arranged, so waiting for it turns a crew into people hoping a community falls out.
drop_if: No disputed or tense moment happens during a filming window without being provoked.
Participants do not want the moment shown.

connections.note: Its occasions list and its aftermath strand are folded into the mended net, where a longer repair can hold both the flare and what follows it.
Two crowds held in one place by something they did not choose.

selection.reason: Its philosophy is sound and is the digest's own leading example for C007, but it depends on an event nobody can schedule; its substance is folded into IDEA-0033, which holds the same occasions over days instead of minutes.

unknowns: No participant or event has been found or confirmed. Everything here is a research direction.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. No location, scene or shot decisions are made at the idea stage.
